variables-s1.title: Records for five shelter dogs
variables-s1.text: An animal shelter keeps one record for each dog in its care. Part of the table is below (invented data).

variables-s2.title: Seniors with part-time jobs
variables-s2.html: District records show that 31% of the 1,250 seniors in a school district have a part-time job. A reporter chooses 80 of the district’s seniors at random and finds that 26% of the 80 have a part-time job. Those with jobs work an average of 14 hours a week (invented data).

items.q: What are the observational units in this table?

why.correct: Each row describes one dog, so the dogs are the observational units.
options: Kennel number is one of the variables recorded about each dog; the rows are dogs.
Right: each row is one dog, and every variable is recorded for each dog.
Those are values of one variable, size group.
Columns are variables. Observational units are what each row describes.
Kennels
The dogs
The size groups small, medium and large
The columns of the table, one for each characteristic

items.q: Which variable is categorical even though its values are numbers?

why.correct: Kennel numbers name places; doing arithmetic with them makes no sense, so the variable is categorical.
options: Weight is a measured amount, so it is quantitative.
A count is quantitative: 2 adoptions is twice as many as 1.
This is categorical, but its values are words, not numbers.
Right: a kennel number is a label. Averaging two kennel numbers gives nothing useful.
Weight (kg)
Times adopted before, a count for each dog
Vaccinated?, recorded as a yes or a no
Kennel number

items.q: How should "Times adopted before" be classified?

why.correct: A count is quantitative, and since it takes whole-number values with gaps between them, it is discrete.
options: Right: it is a count, and counts take separate whole-number values.
A count jumps from 0 to 1 to 2; it does not take every value in between.
Having few values does not make a variable categorical; these values are amounts.
Every variable is recorded for each dog. What matters is whether the values are amounts.
Quantitative and discrete
Quantitative and continuous, like any measurement
Categorical, because it takes just a few different values
Categorical

items.q: Which variable is quantitative and continuous?

why.correct: A continuous variable is measured and can take any value in an interval. Weight is one.
options: A count is discrete: no dog has been adopted 1.5 times.
Kennel numbers are labels, so the variable is categorical.
Right: weight is measured and can take any value in a range, such as 15.1 or 15.13 kg.
Size group puts dogs into groups, so it is categorical even though the groups have an order.
Times adopted before, which takes the values 0, 1 and 2
Kennel number, which runs from 1 up to about 25
Weight (kg)
Size group

items.q: In this situation, what is the 31%?

why.correct: A parameter is a number that describes a population. The 31% describes all 1,250 seniors.
options: A statistic describes a sample. The 31% comes from records on every senior.
A variable is a characteristic of each senior, such as whether that senior has a job.
Right: 31% describes the whole population, all 1,250 seniors in the district.
Observational units are the seniors themselves, not a number about them.
A statistic, because it is written as a percent
A variable
A parameter
An observational unit of the reporter’s study

items.q: In this situation, what is the 26%?

why.correct: A statistic is a number that describes a sample. The 26% describes the 80 seniors chosen.
options: Right: 26% describes the sample of 80 seniors the reporter asked.
It describes only the 80 seniors in the sample, so it is a statistic.
"Has a job" is the variable; 26% is a number that summarizes it for the sample.
The population is the 1,250 seniors; 26% is a number found from the sample.
A statistic
A parameter, because it describes the district’s seniors
A variable
The population that the reporter wants to learn about

items.q: A second reporter chooses a different 80 seniors at random. Which number would most likely be different?

why.correct: A parameter stays fixed. A statistic changes from one sample to the next because different individuals are chosen.
options: The 31% describes the population, which is the same no matter who is sampled.
The district size does not depend on who the reporter chooses.
Both reporters chose 80 seniors; the size of the sample is set in advance.
Right: a statistic depends on which seniors are in the sample, so it changes from sample to sample.
The 31% of the district’s seniors who have a job
The district’s 1,250 seniors
The number of seniors that each reporter asks, which is 80
The percent of the 80 seniors who have a job

items.q: Which of these numbers are statistics? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Numbers found from the 80 sampled seniors are statistics; numbers about all 1,250 seniors are parameters.
options: Right: it describes the sample.
Right: the 14 hours describes the seniors in the sample who have jobs, so it is a statistic.
This describes the population, so it is a parameter.
This describes the population (and is unknown), so it is a parameter.
26% of the 80 seniors have a part-time job
Sampled seniors with jobs work an average of 14 hours a week
31% of the district’s seniors have a part-time job
The average weekly hours of the district’s working seniors

why.correct: A quantitative variable takes numerical values that are amounts. Height is one; jersey numbers and area codes are labels.
options: Jersey numbers are labels; the average jersey number tells you nothing.
Right: height is a measured amount, and averaging heights makes sense.
Favorite sport puts people into groups, so it is categorical.
Area codes are labels for places, so the variable is categorical.
Jersey number printed on the back of each player’s shirt
Height in centimeters
Favorite sport
Phone area code, such as 612 or 858, for each player

items.q: A biologist nets fish in a lake and records each fish’s species and length. What are the observational units?

why.correct: Observational units are the individuals data describe. Each record describes one fish.
options: Right: species and length are recorded for each fish.
Species is a variable recorded about each fish.
Length is another variable; its values are numbers.
The nets are equipment; data are recorded about the fish.
The fish
The species of fish that live in the lake
The lengths, measured in centimeters
The nets

why.correct: A discrete variable is a quantitative variable that takes separate values, usually counts.
options: Time is measured and can take any value in a range, so it is continuous.
Height is continuous; rounding the measurement does not change what kind of variable it is.
Right: a count takes whole-number values with gaps, so it is discrete.
Favorite color is categorical, not quantitative.
The time a student takes to run a mile, in seconds
A student’s height, measured to the nearest millimeter
The number of texts a student sends in a day
Favorite color

items.q: What is the distribution of a variable?

why.correct: A distribution describes all the values a variable takes and how often each value, or range of values, occurs.
options: The most common value is one feature of a distribution, not the whole distribution.
Right: a distribution tells what values occur and how often.
That is the set of observational units, not the distribution of a variable.
That is a measure of how far the values reach, one feature of the distribution.
The single value that the variable takes most often in the data
The values it takes and how often it takes each one
The list of individuals
The difference between the variable’s largest and smallest values

items.q: A league’s official roster lists every player. From it, the average height of all players in the league is 191 cm. A fan measures 12 players and finds an average of 189 cm. Which is correct?

why.correct: A parameter describes a population (the whole league); a statistic describes a sample (the 12 players).
options: This reverses them: the roster covers the whole league, the population.
Whether a number is a parameter or a statistic depends on the group it describes, not on how it is computed.
The 189 describes only the 12 measured players, a sample.
Right: 191 describes every player in the league; 189 describes the 12 measured.
191 cm is a statistic and 189 cm is a parameter
Both are statistics, because both are averages of heights
Both are parameters, because both describe league players
191 cm is a parameter and 189 cm is a statistic

items.q: Which is a variable, not a value of a variable?

why.correct: A variable is a characteristic that can differ from one individual to the next; brown, 1.62 m and yes are values.
options: Brown is one value the variable eye color can take.
Right: eye color is a characteristic recorded for each person.
1.62 meters is a value of the variable height.
Yes is one value of a yes or no variable.
Brown
Eye color
1.62 meters, the height of one student in the class
Yes, one student’s answer to "Do you play an instrument?"

items.q: A survey records five things about each student. Which variables are categorical? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Categorical variables put individuals into groups; quantitative variables record amounts. Grade level is usually treated as a group label here.
options: Right: grade level sorts students into groups. It is coded with numbers, but the analysis counts students in each grade.
Right: yes or no puts each student in a group.
Minutes are a measured amount, so this is quantitative.
A count is quantitative.
Hours of sleep are a measured amount, so this is quantitative.
Grade level (9, 10, 11 or 12)
Whether the student owns a bike
Minutes spent getting to school
Number of siblings
Hours of sleep last night

items.q: Why do researchers usually use a statistic to learn about a parameter?

why.correct: A parameter describes the whole population and is usually unknown. A statistic, from a sample, is used to estimate it.
options: A statistic and a parameter are often found by the same formula; they differ in the group they describe.
It is the statistic that changes from sample to sample; the parameter is fixed.
A sample is smaller than the population, so a statistic describes fewer individuals.
Right: measuring every individual is rarely possible, so a statistic from a sample estimates the parameter.
Statistics are calculated with a different and more accurate formula
A parameter changes each time a new sample is taken
A statistic describes more individuals than a parameter does
The parameter is usually unknown, because it needs data on the whole population
